content.text: Module 11 focuses on the practical nursing skills that appear in both NCLEX clinical scenario questions and Australian OBA OSCE stations. Success in this module is not only about knowing the steps—it is about performing safely, explaining what you are doing, recognising abnormal findings, and escalating appropriately.
Use the following approach for every clinical skill:

items: Prepare: confirm equipment, check infection control requirements.
Identify: confirm patient identity using 3 identifiers and check allergies.
Explain: explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Perform safely: follow the exact steps, avoid contamination, maintain dignity.
Evaluate: reassess findings, document clearly, and escalate if abnormal.

content.text: Tip: During OSCE practice, say your steps out loud. Assessors award marks when they SEE and HEAR safe nursing actions.

items: Perform accurate baseline and focused assessments (vitals, respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological).
Apply infection control and aseptic technique consistently during clinical procedures.
Perform clinical measurements (blood glucose, urinalysis, specimen collection) and interpret results safely.
Administer medications safely across common routes and complete calculations accurately.
Perform basic wound care and implement pressure injury prevention strategies.
Support safe mobility, transfers, and fall prevention using correct manual handling.
Communicate therapeutically, provide patient education, and deliver structured SBAR/ISBAR handover.
Document objectively and report incidents according to professional standards.

content.text: Comprehensive assessment is a core nursing responsibility. In NCLEX, you are tested on recognising cues and acting on abnormal findings. In OSCE, you are assessed on correct technique, patient communication, and accurate reporting.
Vital signs are often the first clue that something is wrong. Always link the measurement to what it means clinically.

items: Temperature: infection, inflammation, heat exposure, adverse drug reactions.
Pulse: tachycardia may indicate pain, fever, dehydration, bleeding, sepsis.
Respirations: a sensitive indicator of deterioration; count a full minute when abnormal.
Blood pressure: hypotension may indicate shock/bleeding; hypertension may indicate pain/anxiety or hypertensive crisis.
Oxygen saturation: low SpO2 indicates respiratory compromise; check probe placement and waveform.
Pain score: use appropriate scale, and reassess after interventions.

content.text: Example (NCLEX-style reasoning): A post-op patient has BP 88/52 and HR 126. This combination suggests possible bleeding or shock. The nurse prioritises assessment of surgical site, level of consciousness, urine output, and escalates urgently.
A structured respiratory assessment includes inspection and auscultation.

items: Inspect: breathing pattern, symmetry, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis.
Auscultate: compare both sides, listen for wheeze (narrowed airways), crackles (fluid), stridor (upper airway emergency).
Assess work of breathing: ability to speak full sentences, position, anxiety/restlessness.

content.text: Red flags: SpO2 < 92% (or facility threshold), RR > 24, stridor, confusion, inability to speak.

items: Chest pain assessment using PQRST (provokes, quality, radiates, severity, time).
Level of consciousness: alert, confused, drowsy, unresponsive.
Motor strength: hand grips, leg strength; compare sides.

content.text: Hand hygiene is the most effective infection prevention action.
Soap and water is required when hands are visibly soiled or for organisms such as C. difficile.

items: Gloves: blood/body fluids, mucous membranes, contaminated equipment.
Keep sterile field above waist and in view.
If contamination occurs, replace contaminated item immediately.

content.text: BGL monitoring is common in OSCE and NCLEX. Always connect the result to patient symptoms.

items: Verify patient identity and explain the procedure.
Prepare equipment and check expiry of strips.
Use correct fingerstick technique and safe sharps disposal.
Interpret result and act on abnormalities; reassess.

content.text: Example: Patient is sweaty and confused; BGL 2.6 mmol/L → treat as hypoglycemia emergency (fast glucose, reassess).

items: Use clean-catch midstream method to reduce contamination.
Label specimen at bedside with correct identifiers.
Interpret: leukocytes/nitrites suggest UTI; ketones suggest poor glucose control.
Record all oral and IV intake.
Measure urine output and alert if low per policy.
Assess for edema, lung crackles, and daily weight changes.
Right patient, medication, dose, route, time.

content.text: Always check allergies, expiry date, and medication integrity before administration.

items: Oral: assess swallowing; sit upright; ensure medication swallowed.
Subcutaneous: insulin/heparin; correct site and technique; safe disposal.
Inhalers/nebulisers: teach technique; reassess respiratory response.

content.text: Use a formula and double-check decimals.

sections.title: Wound Care and Pressure Injury Prevention

items: Signs of infection: redness, warmth, swelling, pus, fever.

content.text: Remove old dressing using clean technique, assess wound, set sterile field, cleanse least to most contaminated, apply dressing, dispose waste, document.

sections.title: Mobility, Manual Handling, and Fall Prevention

items: Assess strength, balance, gait and orthostatic risk.
Explain procedure; use gait belt if available.
Use correct posture; request help/hoist when needed.
Bed low and locked; call bell within reach.

content.text: Use structured communication for escalation: Identification, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.

content.title: Case Study 1 — Vital Signs and Early Deterioration

content.text: Scenario: Post-op patient observations: BP 90/54, HR 128, RR 26, SpO2 91%, pale and sweaty.
Key cues / red flags: Hypotension + tachycardia; Tachypnea; Low SpO2; Diaphoresis suggests shock risk.
Station objectives: Take accurate observations and interpret findings; Initiate immediate actions; Escalate using SBAR.
Checklist (what assessors look for): Hand hygiene + ID; Explain/consent; Accurate vitals; Recognise abnormal findings aloud; Position patient; Apply oxygen per policy; Call help; Reassess.
Expected performance: Show ABC prioritisation and prompt escalation.
Escalation / documentation: Document vitals; notify senior nurse/MO; record SBAR and response.
Pro tips: Say aloud: "These observations are abnormal; I am escalating now."

content.title: Case Study 2 — Blood Glucose and Hypoglycemia

content.text: Scenario: Patient reports dizziness and sweating. BGL is 2.8 mmol/L.
Key cues / red flags: Autonomic symptoms; Low BGL; Risk of seizure/unconsciousness.
Station objectives: Confirm BGL and treat promptly; Reassess and document.
Checklist (what assessors look for): ID + consent; Fingerstick technique; Sharps disposal; Treat with fast glucose; Recheck BGL.
Expected performance: Immediate hypoglycemia treatment and monitoring.
Escalation / documentation: Document BGL values, treatment provided, and patient response; escalate if persistent.
Pro tips: Check swallowing safety; use IV dextrose/glucagon per policy if needed.

content.title: Case Study 3 — Sterile Wound Dressing Change

content.text: Scenario: Surgical wound dressing change required; old dressing has moderate serous drainage.
Key cues / red flags: Risk of contamination; Need sterile field; Monitor for infection.
Station objectives: Perform sterile dressing change; Assess wound and drainage.
Checklist (what assessors look for): Explain/consent; PPE; Remove old dressing (clean); Hand hygiene; Set sterile field; Clean wound; Apply dressing; Dispose waste.
Expected performance: Aseptic technique with accurate wound assessment.
Escalation / documentation: Document wound appearance, drainage amount/type, dressing applied, pain.
Pro tips: If sterile field contaminated, state it and replace items immediately.
Scenario: Administer rapid-acting insulin on sliding scale for BGL 15 mmol/L.
Key cues / red flags: High-alert medication; Risk of hypoglycemia; Need double-check per policy.
Station objectives: Calculate and administer correctly; Educate patient and monitor.
Checklist (what assessors look for): Hand hygiene; 3 identifiers; Allergy check; Confirm insulin type; Dose calculation; Injection site; Skin prep; Sharps disposal; Monitoring.
Expected performance: Safe insulin technique, correct documentation and follow-up.
Escalation / documentation: Document BGL, insulin type/dose/site/time and monitoring plan.
Pro tips: Double-check insulin dose with second nurse if required.

content.title: Case Study 5 — Safe Transfer and Fall Prevention

content.text: Scenario: Older adult unsteady gait needs transfer bed-to-chair.
Key cues / red flags: High fall risk; Orthostatic hypotension risk; Need safe environment.
Station objectives: Assess mobility and complete safe transfer; Prevent fall.
Checklist (what assessors look for): Explain; Non-slip footwear; Lock bed/chair; Clear path; Gait belt/aid; Call bell reachable.
Expected performance: Safe transfer using correct body mechanics.
Escalation / documentation: Document mobility status and fall risk plan.
Pro tips: If dizzy, stop transfer, sit patient, reassess vitals.
Instructions: Choose the safest and most professional response.
Mini Quiz Question 1: RR 28 and SpO2 89% is noted. Priority action?

items: B. Position upright, apply oxygen per policy, escalate

content.text: Correct Answer: B. Rationale: Low SpO2 with tachypnea indicates deterioration. Act using ABCs and escalate.
Mini Quiz Question 2: Which task must NOT be delegated?

items: C. Initial assessment of new admission

content.text: Correct Answer: C. Rationale: Initial assessment requires RN judgement.
Mini Quiz Question 3: Sterile glove touches bed linen. Nurse should:
Correct Answer: B. Rationale: Bed linen is non-sterile; glove contaminated.
Mini Quiz Question 4: Before giving insulin, nurse must first:
Correct Answer: A. Rationale: High-alert medication—ID and allergy checks are essential.
Mini Quiz Question 5: Best patient ID method:
Correct Answer: B. Rationale: Use 2–3 identifiers per policy.
Mini Quiz Question 6: A dizzy patient stands. First action:
Correct Answer: B. Rationale: Prevent fall/injury first.
Mini Quiz Question 7: Most effective infection prevention is:
Correct Answer: B. Rationale: Hand hygiene is the most effective intervention.
Mini Quiz Question 8: In SBAR, the 'R' stands for:
Correct Answer: B. Rationale: SBAR = Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
Mini Quiz Question 9: After treating hypoglycemia, nurse must:
Correct Answer: B. Rationale: Reassessment confirms response and safety.
Mini Quiz Question 10: Objective documentation example is:

items: B. Patient reports pain 8/10 and grimacing noted

content.text: Correct Answer: B. Rationale: Objective charting uses observed facts and quotes.

Answer Review Strategy: For incorrect answers, identify whether the question tested: (1) safety/ABC, (2) infection control/asepsis, (3) medication rights, or (4) communication/documentation. Practise the correct action aloud 3 times.
These learning notes are an educational aid for NCLEX and OBA OSCE preparation and do not replace local clinical policy, supervision, or professional standards.
